lead: Real aircraft sections mix closed cells with open flanges. A wing box may have a closed torque cell and an open trailing-edge flange; a cut-out skin panel is open. The closed cell carries a constant shear flow q<sub>0</sub> round its loop. The open flange has a free edge and carries only the basic flow q<sub>b</sub>. Cut each cell once, treat the skeleton as open, then use compatibility to find q<sub>0</sub>. This mixed case appears in wing ribs, fuselage frames and repair cut-outs. Only a few universities teach it.
prereq: You need: 5.3 for qb and q0, 5.2 for open walls, and 5.5 for cell compatibility.

sections.h3: Mixed sections are cut open cell by cell

blocks.text: A mixed section has one or more closed cells and at least one open wall. The open wall may be a flange, a stringer or a skin panel with a cut-out. The closed cell can carry a constant q0 round its loop. The open wall cannot: it has a free edge, so its shear flow starts at zero and follows qb from 5.2. The closed part also needs qb, found after cutting the cell.

items: Cut every closed cell once at a chosen point. The section becomes an open skeleton.
Find q<sub>b</sub> on the skeleton from the free edges, using the whole section second moment.
Put one unknown q<sub>0</sub> in each closed cell. The open walls get no q<sub>0</sub>.
Impose zero twist on each cell, or equal twist on cells that share a wall.
Add q<sub>b</sub> and q<sub>0</sub> to get the final cell flows. Leave open walls as q<sub>b</sub>.

blocks.where: q<sub>b</sub> is the basic shear flow on the cut cell in N/mm; t is wall thickness in mm; ds is an element of the cell perimeter; the integral goes once round the cell; q<sub>0</sub> is in N/mm.

blocks.text: For one cell, zero twist gives ∮(q<sub>b</sub>+q<sub>0</sub>)/t ds = 0. For two cells i and j sharing a wall, write q<sub>i</sub> and q<sub>j</sub> for the redundant q<sub>0</sub> flows of cells i and j. The shared wall carries q<sub>b</sub>+q<sub>i</sub>−q<sub>j</sub>. For cell i, θ<sub>i</sub> = (1/(2A<sub>i</sub>G))[∮<sub>i</sub>(q<sub>b</sub>/t) ds + q<sub>i</sub>∮<sub>i</sub>(1/t) ds − q<sub>j</sub>∫<sub>shared</sub>(1/t) ds]. For cell j, θ<sub>j</sub> = (1/(2A<sub>j</sub>G))[∮<sub>j</sub>(q<sub>b</sub>/t) ds + q<sub>j</sub>∮<sub>j</sub>(1/t) ds − q<sub>i</sub>∫<sub>shared</sub>(1/t) ds]. Set θ<sub>i</sub> = θ<sub>j</sub>. A<sub>i</sub> and A<sub>j</sub> are enclosed areas; G is shear modulus; q<sub>b</sub> is in N/mm, t in mm, ds in mm, and q<sub>i</sub>, q<sub>j</sub> are in N/mm. Under torque T, a single closed cell has Bredt flow q=T/(2A). An attached open boom carries direct stress from warping and adds no q<sub>0</sub>.

figure.caption: The cut at A turns the cell into an open skeleton; adding q<sub>0</sub> = −17.9 N/mm gives the final cell flows, while the flange reaches 19.6 N/mm at A.

spec.title: Mixed section method
spec.aria: A block diagram shows cutting a closed cell, finding basic shear flow, adding one unknown q0, imposing compatibility, and forming the final shear flow.

examples.question: A section has one rectangular cell 150 mm × 80 mm with 2 mm walls and an open flange 60 mm long and 2 mm thick attached at one corner. The flange runs horizontally outward from corner A. It carries a vertical shear force of 6 kN. Find the shear flow in the cell walls and in the open flange.
steps: Take A(0,0), B(150,0), C(150,80), D(0,80); flange E(−60,0) to A. Cut the cell at A. All walls are t=2 mm. Positive cell direction is A→B→C→D→A; flange direction is E→A.
Use q<sub>b</sub>=−(V/I<sub>xx</sub>)∫t y ds, with y from the centroid. Flange at A: q<sub>b</sub>=19.6 N/mm. Cell: AB goes 0→49.0, BC to 45.6, CD to −16.2, DA to −19.6 N/mm.
Zero twist: ∮(q<sub>b</sub>+q<sub>0</sub>)/t ds=0. Cell perimeter P=2(150+80)=460 mm; ∮q<sub>b</sub> ds=8229 N. So q<sub>0</sub>=−8229/460=−17.9 N/mm.
Final cell flow is q=q<sub>b</sub>+q<sub>0</sub>; flange flow stays q<sub>b</sub>. AB: A −17.9, B 31.1. BC: C 27.7. CD: D −34.1. DA: A −37.5. Flange A: 19.6 N/mm.
examples.answer: q<sub>0</sub> = −17.9 N/mm; cell flows range from −37.5 to 31.1 N/mm; the open flange reaches 19.6 N/mm at the corner.
examples.check:
b=150.0
h=80.0
t=2.0
Lf=60.0
V=6000.0
L_EA=Lf
L_AB=b
L_BC=h
L_CD=b
L_DA=h
Ltot=L_EA+L_AB+L_BC+L_CD+L_DA
xbar=(L_EA*(-Lf/2)+L_AB*(b/2)+L_BC*b+L_CD*(b/2)+L_DA*0)/Ltot
ybar=(L_BC*(h/2)+L_CD*h+L_DA*(h/2))/Ltot
I=t*L_EA*(0-ybar)**2 + t*L_AB*(0-ybar)**2 + t*L_CD*(h-ybar)**2
I+=t*(L_BC*(h/2-ybar)**2 + L_BC**3/12)
I+=t*(L_DA*(h/2-ybar)**2 + L_DA**3/12)
k=V/I*t
q_flange_A=k*ybar*Lf
q_B=k*ybar*b
q_C=q_B-k*(h*h/2-ybar*h)
q_D=q_C-k*(h-ybar)*b
q_A_cell=q_D-k*((h-ybar)*h-h*h/2)
I_AB=0.5*q_B*b
I_BC=q_B*h-k*(h**3/6-ybar*h*h/2)
I_CD=q_C*b-0.5*k*(h-ybar)*b*b
I_DA=q_D*h-k*((h-ybar)*h*h/2-h**3/6)
sumq=I_AB+I_BC+I_CD+I_DA
q0=-sumq/(2*(b+h))
q_AB_B=q_B+q0
q_BC_C=q_C+q0
q_CD_D=q_D+q0
q_DA_A=q_A_cell+q0
print(f"{I:.0f}")
print(f"{q0:.1f}")
print(f"{q_flange_A:.1f}")
print(f"{q_AB_B:.1f}")
print(f"{q_BC_C:.1f}")
print(f"{q_CD_D:.1f}")
print(f"{q_DA_A:.1f}")

traps: Treating the mixed section as one closed tube and using Bredt for shear. The open flange has no enclosed area.
Leaving the open flange out of I<sub>xx</sub>. Its direct stress changes q<sub>b</sub> everywhere.
Adding q<sub>0</sub> to the open flange. q<sub>0</sub> exists only round a closed cell.

Using equal twist between a cell and an open flange. An open flange has no enclosed area and no independent Bredt circulation q<sub>0</sub>, so it does not give a separate closed-cell twist equation. It twists with the section but does not impose a closed-loop compatibility condition.
Reversing the chosen cell loop and keeping the sign of q<sub>0</sub>. Reverse all signed cell flows with the loop.

quiz.a: A constant shear flow added round a closed cell after the cell is cut.

quiz.q: Why cut a closed cell before finding q<sub>b</sub>?
quiz.a: It becomes an open skeleton, so q<sub>b</sub> follows from a free edge.

quiz.q: In the example, q<sub>b</sub> at B is 49.0 N/mm and q<sub>0</sub>=−17.9 N/mm. Find final q at B.
Why is zero twist imposed on the cell but not on the open flange?
quiz.a: An open flange has no enclosed area and no independent Bredt circulation q<sub>0</sub>, so it does not give a separate closed-cell twist equation. It twists with the section but does not impose a closed-loop compatibility condition.

quiz.q: State the zero-twist condition for one cell.
What equation links two cells that share a wall?
quiz.a: Their twist rates are equal; the shared wall carries q<sub>i</sub>−q<sub>j</sub>.

quiz.q: Why is Bredt alone wrong for this section?
quiz.a: Bredt gives a constant flow in a closed tube; it ignores the open flange's direct stress and free-edge q<sub>b</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real wing boxes combine closed torque cells with open leading-edge cut-outs and trailing-edge flanges. Finite-element models recover the same cut-cell q<sub>0</sub> as compatibility constraints between cells. Search 'shear flow combined open closed section', 'cut cell compatibility', and 'Bredt-Batho open boom'.
